meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Resentment is like drinking poison and then hoping it will kill your enemies'?
meta.ogDescription: Nelson Mandela never wrote it. It's a modern proverb rooted in 1980s Christian/self-help writing with recovery-circle currency in the 1990s — no Mandela speech, book, or letter contains the line.

answer.label: Not Nelson Mandela — a modern proverb he never wrote
answer.authorDates: Concise form documented from the mid-1990s; roots in 1980s Christian/self-help writing
answer.sourceLine: No speech, book, letter, or interview by Mandela contains this line. Quote Investigator ↗ traces the “resentment / poison” figure to an evolving saying — an early strong match is Bert Ghezzi’s 1980 The Angry Christian, with the crisp modern wording appearing among several writers in the 1990s — and finds no evidence Mandela originated it.

source.heading: An evolved proverb, pinned on Mandela later
source.excerpt: “Resentment is like drinking poison and then hoping it will kill your enemies.”
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ finds the figure evolved over decades and credits no single author, naming Bert Ghezzi’s 1980 The Angry Christian as an early strong match.
Word-nerd chronicler Barry Popik ↗ documents 1990s appearances from Susan Cheever and Malachy McCourt, and notes USA Today only folded it into a Mandela list in December 2013.
The exact “kill your enemies” Mandela wording is reproduced across quote aggregators like Goodreads ↗, none of which cite a Mandela source.
source.excerptNote: The wording circulates in many variants — “taking poison and waiting for the other person to die,” “…hoping it’ll kill someone else” — long predating its attachment to Mandela.
source.rightsNote: This is an anonymous modern proverb with no single identifiable first-publication, so no copyright status can be responsibly asserted for the exact wording. Individual later renderings (e.g. Bert Ghezzi’s 1980 phrasing, or Carrie Fisher’s 2003 novel) are in copyright to their own authors, but none is the “drinking poison…kill your enemies” line credited to Mandela.

author.name: Nelson Mandela
author.heading: Why it lands on Mandela
author.bio: Nelson Mandela spent 27 years imprisoned under apartheid and emerged to lead South Africa’s peaceful transition, serving as its first democratically elected president (1994–1999) and winning the Nobel Peace Prize. His public embrace of reconciliation over vengeance made him a natural magnet for uplifting sayings about forgiveness — but living a proverb is not the same as writing it, and this particular line traces to sources that predate his association with it.

copyAttribution: Contrary to popular belief, Nelson Mandela did not write "Resentment is like drinking poison and then hoping it will kill your enemies." It is a modern proverb that evolved through recovery and self-help writing in the 1980s–90s; Quote Investigator finds no Mandela source for it.

misattribution.heading: The misattribution
misattribution.intro: A clever line about forgiveness, a globally beloved reconciliation figure — the pairing is irresistible and unsourced. Here is what the record actually shows.

items.why: No Mandela speech, autobiography, letter, or interview has ever been shown to contain this line. Quote Investigator ↗ finds no evidence he originated it, and Barry Popik ↗ notes it was only bundled into a Mandela quote list around his December 2013 death.

items.who: Carrie Fisher, Malachy McCourt, Alan Brandt & others
items.why: The concise saying surfaces under several names in the 1990s — Alan Brandt and Susan Cheever (1995), Malachy McCourt in a 1998 New York Times profile — and Carrie Fisher used it in her 2003 novel The Best Awful, per Quote Investigator ↗. None is the single originator.

Quote Investigator ↗ identifies Bert Ghezzi’s 1980 book The Angry Christian — “Resentment is like a poison we carry around inside us…” — as an early strong match, part of an evolving proverb, not a coining of the exact modern line.

misattribution.truthLine: It’s a modern proverb that grew out of recovery and self-help writing across the 1980s–90s — not a Mandela quotation. See Quote Investigator’s full account ↗.

context.heading: Why the myth sticks
lead: The saying works because its image is exact: harming yourself in the name of harming someone else. That moral clarity is why it gets attached to figures famous for transcending grievance — and no one fits that story better than Nelson Mandela.
But the documented trail runs through recovery literature and 1990s writers, not Robben Island. Mandela embodied the idea; he did not author the sentence.
detailsBody: Common forms include “taking poison and waiting for the other person to die” and “hoping it’ll kill someone else.” The “kill your enemies” phrasing is the one most often stamped with Mandela’s name.
Some tellings swap “resentment” for “hatred” or “holding a grudge” — further evidence of an oral, evolving proverb rather than a fixed quotation.
context.pull: Living a proverb is not the same as writing it.
